segments.title: Why theorists begin with the Seven Years' War
segments.body: The Seven Years' War is a frequent starting point for military theorists. It is arguably the first world war. A further argument is that it was the first conflict to contain nearly every kind of strategic case. This breadth helps explain its appeal as a historical example for strategic theory.

evidence.note: The introduction calls the war a possible first world war and says it contains every kind of strategic case.

segments.summary: The Seven Years' War's global scope and variety of strategic examples help explain its appeal to military theorists.

segments.title: Land and maritime arguments from the Seven Years' War
segments.body: Arguments for a land strategy can draw on the war's mass armies and large forces fighting ashore. A case for maritime strategy can draw on its operations across the globe and the range of factors they involve. The same conflict therefore supplies examples for both strategic approaches.

evidence.note: The Seven Years' War supports arguments drawn from both mass armies ashore and globe-spanning maritime strategy.

segments.summary: The Seven Years' War can support arguments about mass armies ashore as well as maritime strategy across a global theatre.

segments.title: Why the Seven Years' War suits selective historical arguments
segments.body: Many theorists approach the Seven Years' War with an argument already in mind and seek historical illustration rather than an open-ended lesson. By the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the war's name was familiar even though many of its actors and details were not. That combination made it harder for an audience to challenge a theorist with awkward context or nuance. A seemingly clean historical example may look persuasive because its complications are less widely known.

evidence.note: Theorists could use the familiar name of the Seven Years' War while relying on an audience's weaker knowledge of its context and nuance.

segments.summary: The Seven Years' War was familiar by name while its details were less widely known, making selective historical examples harder to challenge.

segments.title: Why grand strategy cannot be purely maritime or continental
segments.body: Broad strategic formulas become less convincing once the particular context of a country and war is examined. As with economic policy, a strategy suited to a country's circumstances often needs a mixture of measures. No country can afford a wholly maritime strategy, and probably no country can afford a wholly continental one. A state may make one approach its overarching priority, but it must still understand the other and remain prepared to exert some influence through it.

evidence.note: The closing argument says strategic thinking runs into context and rejects wholly pure maritime or continental strategies.

segments.summary: A state may lean maritime or continental, but a strategy suited to its circumstances still requires attention to the other sphere.
